title: US Proposes $70,000 OPT Fee That Could Hit Indian Students Hardest
excerpt: A DHS proposal would charge universities $70,000 for a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for any subsequent OPT, including STEM extensions. It is not in effect, and comments close November 9, 2026.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has proposed a $70,000 fee for a student's first Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation, and $30,000 for any subsequent OPT, including the 24-month STEM extension.
  • The fee is not in effect. It is a notice of proposed rulemaking published October 8, 2026 (Federal Register document 2026-20660, docket ICEB-2026-0100), with public comments due by November 9, 2026.
  • What this means for you: nothing is owed today, and students already recommended for OPT are not covered. If finalized, schools could pass the cost to F-1 students or employers, so Fall 2027 applicants should ask target universities directly whether they would pass it on and budget for that scenario.
  • India sent 363,019 students to the US in 2024-25, and 143,740 Indians were on OPT, the group most exposed to the change.

Indian students hoping to work in the United States after graduation could see their universities charged $70,000 each for Optional Practical Training under a Department of Homeland Security proposal published in the Federal Register on October 8, according to IANS reporting carried by hi INDiA.

The proposed rule, titled Optional Practical Training Fees, would set "$70,000 for initial OPT; and $30,000 for any subsequent OPT" for each F-1 student through a Student and Exchange Visitor Program-certified institution. The subsequent fee would apply to the 24-month STEM OPT extension. A student who uses both pre-completion and post-completion OPT would face a total of $100,000, compared with $70,000 if the entire OPT period falls after graduation.

How the fee would work

The fee would be paid by the institution before a designated school official recommends a student for OPT in SEVIS, the federal system that tracks student visa holders. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services would not grant employment authorization if the fee had not been paid. Changing employers during OPT would not trigger a new fee, and schools could seek a refund if the student does not receive an employment authorization document. Once that document is issued, the fee is not refunded.

DHS acknowledges in the proposal that schools may pass the financial obligation on to F-1 students, all students, or employers. That pass-through is the central practical question for Indian families: a charge that is legally owed by a university could still end up in a student's budget, an employer's offer, or a broader tuition pool. Today, by contrast, students pay only the USCIS filing fee for Form I-765, $470 online or $520 on paper, and schools pay nothing for an OPT recommendation, according to Collegedunia's analysis of the proposal.

"Reduce the rampant fraud and abuse of OPT"

— Department of Homeland Security, stated purpose of the proposed OPT fees rule

Why DHS says it is proposing the fee

DHS says the fee would reduce fraud and abuse in OPT, protect U.S. workers, and ease the burden of OPT investigations, and discourage use of OPT to bypass H-1B caps and wage requirements. DHS cites 194,554 OPT and 95,384 STEM OPT participants in 2024, and projects annualized transfers of $12.8 billion, with 10-year transfers of $109.4 billion.

Collegedunia's summary notes Homeland Security Investigations flagged more than 10,000 F-1 students at suspect employers, and DHS argues the payroll-tax exemption for F-1 workers gives employers a cost reason to hire students.

Why India is most exposed

Indians are the largest group of international students in the United States, and OPT is the usual bridge from a U.S. degree to an H-1B job. Open Doors data cited in coverage put Indian enrollment at 363,019 in 2024-25, about 31 percent of all international students, with 143,740 Indians participating in OPT, up 47.3 percent from the previous year.

Universities weighing a $70,000 charge may limit OPT support, particularly for non-STEM courses, where DHS assumes institutions may be less likely to pay for a single year. Two schools could treat the same Indian student very differently, depending on whether they absorb or pass on the fee.

What happens next

The proposal is not law. Comments must be received by November 9, 2026, under docket ICEB-2026-0100 through the Federal eRulemaking Portal at regulations.gov; comments sent by email or letter will not be considered, according to the Federal Register notice. A separate information-collection comment period runs to December 7, 2026. DHS must review comments before issuing any final rule, and no implementation date has been set. Under the proposal, a final rule would take effect 60 days after publication and would apply only to OPT recommendations dated on or after that effective date.

The proposal arrives on top of the $100,000 H-1B fee policy now in litigation. For Fall 2027 applicants, the concrete steps are to submit any comment through regulations.gov before November 9 and ask each target university in writing whether it would pass an OPT fee to students if the rule is finalized.
